# Story Bible — Maya in Kochi (Malayalam track, continuity ground-truth)

Canonical facts the storyboard reviewer checks a new week against. Updated as each week is locked.
The Kochi instantiation of the shared arc: same protagonist and story skeleton as the Danish course,
authored natively in Malayalam.

## Maya (protagonist)
- From Mexico. A **software engineer** — she moved to Kochi in **January** because she landed a job
  at a software company here; the job is *why* she came. 31 when she arrived; turns 32 the following
  summer. Gradually settling in.
- First-person narrator throughout.

## Timeline & seasons
- Arrives **January** — Kochi's pleasant dry season. The year builds through the **March–May heat**
  and breaks into the **June monsoon**.

## Recurring cast
- **Anitha** — Malayali neighbour, met day 1 (week 1), Maya's first friend; lives in the same building.
  Kind, helpful.
- **Prakash** — a colleague at Maya's software company (met on her first day, week 2). Use him when a
  work colleague is needed rather than an anonymous colleague.
- **Family** — back home in Mexico, contact by video call: parents, sister **Sofía**, brother
  **Diego**, and the family dog **Lola**.

## Cross-cutting rules (every week)
- **Register** — polite.
- **Privacy** — her ID/registration numbers are sensitive: never read aloud digit-by-digit. Phone
  numbers may be shared; any phone number is an obvious placeholder, never plausibly real.
- **Numbers said aloud are Malayalam words, not digits** — this is an audio course. Currency is
  **rupees**, spelled as words. Numbers woven into action, not drilled.
- **Setting is authentically Kochi** — local places, food, weather, and transit are the point of this
  track; no need to genericize.
- **Dialogue** — other characters speak *to* Maya, never in her first-person voice.
- **Cast used sparingly** — do not force recurring cast into scenes; a week may stand on its own.
- **The story never depicts Maya *learning* Malayalam** — she simply lives her life in it.

## Status ledger — what is TRUE by end of each week
(filled in as weeks are built)

transition is NOT a contradiction.

### [Week 1 · Scene 1 · 01_airport_arrival]
I am now outside the airport.
It is the month of January.
There is gentle heat and a breeze here.
There is a woman near me.
She is another passenger.
She looks at me and smiles.
"What is your name?" she asks.
"My name is Maya," I say.
"Where are you from?" she asks.
"I am from Mexico."
She is a very nice woman.
"Welcome to Kochi," she says.
Kochi is a new city to me.
This is a good place.
My new life is here.

There is a taxi there.
I put my big bag in the taxi.
I get into the taxi.
The driver looks at me.
"Madam, where is the place?" he asks.
I give him my new address.
"Is it Kakkanad?" he asks.
"Yes, my flat is in Kakkanad," I say.
The taxi goes forward.
"Where are you from?" he asks.
"I am from Mexico," I say.
"Is it Mexico? Very good, madam," he says.
The taxi is going to Kakkanad.

### [Week 1 · Scene 3 · 03_suitcase_struggle]
This is my new apartment.
I am in front of the building now.
My suitcase is very big.
It is very heavy.
I pull the suitcase inside the building.
This is a big struggle.
Where is my room?
I look for my door.
Ah, the room is here.
This is my door.
I have the key in my hand.
I insert the key into the door.
I open the door.
I push the suitcase inside.
I enter the room.
It is dark in the room.
I am very tired.
Still, I am in Kochi.
I smile in the dark.

### [Week 1 · Scene 4 · 04_ceiling_fan]
This is my new room.
It is very warm here.
There is a switch on the wall.
I flick that switch.
The ceiling fan spins above.
Now there is a breeze in the room.
I feel a great relief.
I walk around the room.
I look around.
There is a bed here.
It is a very comfortable bed.
There is a table there.
It is a sturdy table.
There is a computer in my bag.
That table is for my computer.
This room is small.
Even so, I like it very much.
This is my home in Kochi.

### [Week 1 · Scene 5 · 05_green_city]
Now it is morning.
I am near the window.
I open the window.
I look outside.
Kochi is very beautiful.
This is a green city.
There are many trees outside.
These trees are very green.
Now it is the month of January.
It is good weather here.
The wind comes through the window.
It is a good sea breeze.
The wind touches my face.
For a moment, I remember Mexico.
Mexico is my own homeland.
I remember the streets there.
My phone is on the table.
I will call my family in the evening.
Now I enjoy this good breeze.

### [Week 1 · Scene 6 · 06_calling_mom]
It is evening in Kochi now.
There is a bed in my room.
I sit on the bed.
I call my mother.
Mom is in Mexico.
"Hello Maya," Mom says.
"Mom, I am in Kochi," I say.
"Are you in the flat?" Mom asks.
"Yes Mom, I am in my flat," I say.
"Is everything safe there?" Mom asks.
"Yes, I am safe here," I say.
"Do you have a good job there?" Mom asks.
"Yes Mom, I have a good job here," I say.
"Where are Sofia and Diego?" I ask.
"They are here," Mom says.
"Our dog Lola is also here," Mom says.
I smile happily.
I hang up the phone.

### [Week 1 · Scene 7 · 07_meeting_anitha]
I open my door.
I step outside.
The next door opens.
There is a woman there.
She smiles.
"Hello, are you new?" she asks.
"Yes, I am new here," I say.
"My name is Anitha," she says.
"What is your name?"
"My name is Maya," I say.
"Where are you from?" Anitha asks.
"I am from Mexico."
"Mexico!"
"Is that very far?"
"Yes, it is very far."
"Do you have a job here?" Anitha asks.
"Yes, I am a software engineer."
Anitha is very happy.
"Welcome to Kochi!" she says.
Anitha is a very kind woman.
I now have a friend here.

### [Week 1 · Scene 8 · 08_family_photo]
I come back to my room.
My big suitcase is on the floor.
I open the suitcase.
My clothes are in it.
I take the clothes out.
There is a photo in the suitcase.
That is my family's photo.
This is my sister.
Her name is Sofia.
This is my brother.
His name is Diego.
There is also a dog in the photo.
That is our dog.
Her name is Lola.
I put that photo on the table.
Now my computer and the photo are on the table.
My family is in Mexico.
But now they are with me.
I smile.

### [Week 1 · Scene 9 · 09_bedtime_routine]
It is night now.
I am very tired.
This is my small bathroom.
There is a mirror here.
I brush my teeth.
I wash my face.
The water is very cold.
I go to the bedroom.
There is a good bed here.
I lie down on the bed.
There is a ceiling fan above.
I hear the sound of the fan.
I take my phone.
I set the morning alarm.
Tomorrow is my second day in Kochi.
Tomorrow is a new day.
I like it here very much.
I am going to sleep now.
Good night.

### [Week 2 · Scene 1 · 01_office_arrival]
I arrive at the office.
Today is my first day.
It is the month of January.
The morning weather is nice.
I walk to the front desk.
A security guard is there.
"Good morning, madam," the guard says.
"Good morning," I reply.
"I have a new job here," I say.
"Does madam have an ID card?" the guard asks.
"No, I do not have an ID card," I reply.
The guard gives me a big logbook.
"Does madam have a pen?" the guard asks.
"Yes, I have a pen," I say.
I write my name in the book.
The time is nine o'clock.
The guard gives me a temporary ID badge.
"Thank you," I say.
I go inside the office.

### [Week 2 · Scene 2 · 02_meeting_prakash]
I stand in the bright lobby of the office.
A person comes towards me.
He smiles at me.
"Hello, are you Maya?" he asks.
I say yes.
"I am Prakash," he says.
"Welcome to our team."
I thank Prakash.
We walk into the main room.
It is a very big room.
Fifty people work here.
Prakash stands near a large window.
"This is your desk," Prakash says.
I look at my new desk.
I have a good chair there.
I have a big monitor too.
"Do you have any questions now?" Prakash asks.
"I do not have questions now," I say.
The January sunlight comes through the window.
I feel very happy.

### [Week 2 · Scene 3 · 03_missing_phone_number]
I sit at my desk.
I open my new laptop.
Prakash stands near me.
He helps me.
"We have a team directory," Prakash says.
"There are twelve people in our team."
"Everyone's phone number is in it."
I look at the computer screen.
"Maya, do you have an Indian phone number?" Prakash asks.
I look at my phone.
"No, I do not have an Indian phone number," I say.
"I have a Mexican number."
"I do not have an Indian SIM card."
Prakash nods.
"Do you need a new SIM card?" he asks.
"Yes, I need a SIM card today," I say.
"There is a mobile shop outside the office," Prakash says.
I write down the name of that mobile shop.
I continue my work.

### [Week 2 · Scene 4 · 04_mobile_shop]
I cross the road.
It is lunch time.
I do not have an Indian phone number.
There is a small mobile shop there.
I enter the shop.
The shopkeeper looks at me.
I say, 'Hello, I want a new SIM.'
He asks, 'Is it a prepaid connection?'
I say, 'Yes, it is prepaid.'
He asks, 'Do you have documents?'
I say, 'Yes, I have a passport.'
I have a visa too.
I give the company's letter to him as well.
He looks at all the documents.
He says, 'Everything is correct.'
He says, 'This is one hundred rupees.'
I give one hundred rupees.
He gives the new SIM to me.
I put the SIM in my bag.
I walk back to the office.

### [Week 2 · Scene 5 · 05_sim_activation]
I am in the mobile shop.
The shopkeeper looks at my passport.
He types on the computer.
He gives me a form.
I have a pen.
I sign the paper.
He takes a new SIM card.
"The price is fifty rupees," he says.
I give him the money.
He gives the SIM card to me.
"Does this have a network now?" I ask.
"No, this does not have a network now," he says.
"A foreign passport takes time," he says.
"It takes two hours," he explains.
I safely put the SIM card in my bag.
I walk out of the shop.
There is bright sunlight outside.
I cross the road.
I go back to the office.
My afternoon work starts again.

### [Week 2 · Scene 6 · 06_registration_commute]
Today there is good sunshine in Kochi.
I go to the government office today.
I get into a yellow auto.
"Where are you going?" the driver asks.
"To the Foreigners Registration Office," I say.
The auto goes fast.
I look outside.
There is a lot of traffic in the city.
I have a big file in my hand.
There are important documents in the file.
I have the original passport.
I have the visa too.
I have five photos.
I do not have a phone number right now.
But, I do not have fear.
The auto reaches in front of the office.
The meter shows eighty rupees.
I open my bag.
I give eighty rupees to the driver.
I walk into the office.

### [Week 2 · Scene 7 · 07_waiting_for_token]
I am in a government office.
The office is very busy.
A lot of people are here.
I am sitting on a chair.
I have a token.
The token number is forty-two.
I am waiting patiently.
I am not in a hurry now.
Time is passing slowly.
A clerk is sitting at the counter.
The clerk calls the next number.
"Token number forty-two!"
I stand up immediately.
I walk to the wooden counter.
I give my token to the clerk.
The clerk looks at me.
I open my file.
I am a little nervous.

### [Week 2 · Scene 8 · 08_document_submission]
I stand in front of the counter.
The official looks at me.
He asks me.
"Do you have your passport?"
I politely reply.
"Yes, I have my passport."
He asks again.
"Do you have proof of address?"
I say, "Yes, I have everything with me."
I give two important documents to him.
He checks those documents.
He adds the information into the computer.
A little time passes.
The official tells me.
"Your application is processing online now."
I have great relief now.

### [Week 2 · Scene 9 · 09_celebratory_snack]
I come out of the government office.
I am very happy now.
All my main errands are finished.
There is a small thattukada on the side of the road.
There is a good crowd there.
There are four people in front of the shop.
I walk to that thattukada.
I get the smell of tea.
I ask the vendor, "Brother, I want one hot tea."
The vendor asks, "Is tea alone enough?"
I look at the snacks there.
There is nice hot pazhampori there.
"I want one pazhampori too," I say.
The vendor quickly makes the tea.
He gives me tea in a glass.
He gives the pazhampori on a small plate too.
I drink that hot tea.
I eat the pazhampori.
It has a very good taste.

### [Week 2 · Scene 10 · 10_messaging_home]
I stand in front of the thattukada.
The vendor gives me hot tea and pazhampori.
"The total is thirty rupees," he says to me.
I give him thirty rupees.
I drink the tea.
The tea is very hot.
The pazhampori is very tasty.
I take my new phone.
The phone now has a network.
Now I have a new number.
I send a message to my family.
They are in Mexico.
"I have a new number," I write.
My sister Sofía quickly sends a reply.
She sends me a picture of Lola.
Lola is our dog.
I look at that picture.
I smile very happily.
I am very happy now.

  summer. Gradually settling in.

- From Mexico. A **software engineer** — she moved to Kochi in **January** because she landed a job

  summer. Gradually settling in.

# Story Bible — Maya in Kochi (Malayalam track, continuity ground-truth)

authored natively in Malayalam.

## Maya (protagonist)
- From Mexico. A **software engineer** — she moved to Kochi in **January** because she landed a job
  at a software company here; the job is *why* she came. 31 when she arrived; turns 32 the following
  summer. Gradually settling in.
- First-person narrator throughout.

## Timeline & seasons
- Arrives **January** — Kochi's pleasant dry season. The year builds through the **March–May heat**
  and breaks into the **June monsoon**.

## Recurring cast
- **Anitha** — Malayali neighbour, met day 1 (week 1), Maya's first friend; lives in the same building.
  Kind, helpful.

  work colleague is needed rather than an anonymous colleague.

- **Register** — polite.

## Maya (protagonist)
- From Mexico. A **software engineer** — she moved to Kochi in **January** because she landed a job
  at a software company here; the job is *why* she came. 31 when she arrived; turns 32 the following
  summer. Gradually settling in.
- First-person narrator throughout.

## Timeline & seasons
- Arrives **January** — Kochi's pleasant dry season. The year builds through the **March–May heat**
  and breaks into the **June monsoon**.

- **Anitha** — Malayali neighbour, met day 1 (week 1), Maya's first friend; lives in the same building.

# Story Bible — Maya in Kochi (Malayalam track, continuity ground-truth)

Canonical facts the storyboard reviewer checks a new week against. Updated as each week is locked.
The Kochi instantiation of the shared arc: same protagonist and story skeleton as the Danish course,
authored natively in Malayalam.

## Maya (protagonist)
- From Mexico. A **software engineer** — she moved to Kochi in **January** because she landed a job
  at a software company here; the job is *why* she came. 31 when she arrived; turns 32 the following
  summer. Gradually settling in.
- First-person narrator throughout.

## Timeline & seasons
- Arrives **January** — Kochi's pleasant dry season. The year builds through the **March–May heat**
  and breaks into the **June monsoon**.

## Recurring cast
- **Anitha** — Malayali neighbour, met day 1 (week 1), Maya's first friend; lives in the same building.
  Kind, helpful.
- **Prakash** — a colleague at Maya's software company (met on her first day, week 2). Use him when a
  work colleague is needed rather than an anonymous colleague.
- **Family** — back home in Mexico, contact by video call: parents, sister **Sofía**, brother
  **Diego**, and the family dog **Lola**.

## Cross-cutting rules (every week)
- **Register** — polite.
- **Privacy** — her ID/registration numbers are sensitive: never read aloud digit-by-digit. Phone
  numbers may be shared; any phone number is an obvious placeholder, never plausibly real.
  Maya's mobile: **98765 43210** (spoken as Malayalam number words when read aloud).
- **Numbers said aloud are Malayalam words, not digits** — this is an audio course. Currency is
  **rupees**, spelled as words. Numbers woven into action, not drilled.
- **Setting is authentically Kochi** — local places, food, weather, and transit are the point of this
  track; no need to genericize.
- **Dialogue** — other characters speak *to* Maya, never in her first-person voice.
- **Cast used sparingly** — do not force recurring cast into scenes; a week may stand on its own.
- **The story never depicts Maya *learning* Malayalam** — she simply lives her life in it.
